newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish lignite mine head resigns, strike suspended.
newsitem.headline: Polish lignite mine head resigns, strike suspended.

text.p: Workers at Poland's largest lignite mine, state-owned KWP Belchatow, suspended a strike on Tuesday after the company's head resigned, the strike committee official said.
The six-day-old strike aimed at ousting Belchatow's director Jerzy Wagenknecht has idled the nearby power plant, which produces about 25 percent of Poland's electricity.

"We appreciate the director's gesture and we are restoring lignite supplies to the Belchatow plant. But our protest will continue until a new director meets our other demands," Ryszard Galka, a strike committee member told Reuters over telephone.
Galka said the workers demanded improvements in working conditions, payment for the period of the strike and assurances that the strike organisers would not be punished.

The strike in Belchatow, central Poland, has not caused cuts of power supply as a previous one did in 1993. But energy-sector officials said industry would have faced power shortages if temperatures had falled below zero.
Economy Minister Wieslaw Kaczmarek sharply criticised the strike, calling it "unions' bargaining which could put the national energy security under threat."
The unions have accused Wagenknecht of violating labour agreements and mismanagement.
Some analysts said that Wagenkneht's resignation was a bad sign for the Polish economy because it showed how strong unions were in Poland's major industries.

"I do not know who is right in this conflict, but it is most unhealthy that the workforce decides about the fate of a company which ranks among Poland's top 20," said Bohdan Wyznikiewicz, a senior analysts at the independent Gdansk Market Economy Research Institute.
"It is a signal for major enterprises, both for workers and managements, that if there is a conflict, the workforce is potentially a stronger side," he added.
